newsitem.title: UK: Latam's ballooning reserves may eliminate Bradys.
newsitem.headline: Latam's ballooning reserves may eliminate Bradys.

text.p: A staggering increase in the international reserves of major Latin American states means they are now positioned to shed the stigma of default by eliminating their high yielding Brady bonds, analysts said on Thursday.
Since the end of 1989 international reserve holdings, excluding gold, of Latin America's six biggest Brady countries have more than quintupled -- from $21 billion in 1989 to $111 billion at present.

"International liquidity (excluding gold) of $111 billion is not far short of Latin America's total Brady issue of $122 billion and exceeds the market value of the Brady issue," said Paul Luke, Deutsche Morgan Grenfell's head of emerging market research.

"This comfortable liquidity position, itself in part a reflection of the ability of Latin America to attract external finance...means that these countries are well placed to buy back their high-yielding external obligations," he said.

With some additional financing these countries could probably eliminate their Brady bonds altogether, while the impetus to retire them should make them an attractive investment in the meantime, he added.
Richard Gray, emerging markets analyst at Bankamerica, agreed but with reservations.
"The high level of reserves does facilitate this process, but I would watch the quality of reserves," he said.
He pointed to the high component of "hot money" within Brazil's reserve basket, adding it would be dangerous to commit such short-term money to buying back long-term instruments.

The biggest reserves' jump took place in Brazil, where 1989's $17.5 billion is now brushing $60 million. Argentina recorded the biggest proportional increase with reserves up twelve-fold over the same period, while Peru has seen a tenfold rise.
Ecuador, Mexico and Venezuela have all seen their reserves double or triple.
"The scale of the increase is quite staggering in comparison with other countries," Luke said.

Earlier this year Mexico set a precedent in attempting to retire some of its collateralised Brady bonds -- restructured commercial debt issued to replace defaulted commercial loans of the 1980s. It has also used the proceeds from recent long-dated global bond issues to buy back $1.2 billion of its own Brady debt at face value.
Since then the Philippines has exchanged some of its Bradys for a fresh 20-year bond, while Brazil has passed legislation allowing it to replace its Bradys with global bonds.
Peru, in the process of a Brady bond restructuring, said earlier this month it too planned to buy back some of its commercial debt. Some analysts say it has already done so.
Market players are now speculating on whether Argentina and Venezuela, riding high after windfall oil revenues due to recent troubles in Iraq, will follow suit.

In London earlier this week Nicholas Brady, the father of the Brady plan that restored credibility to Latin America after the 1980s debt crisis, said he envisaged the elimination of these bonds as a sign of progress among the Brady nations.
Luke's colleague, analyst Stuart Parkinson, said the level of reserves was good news for the image of these nations abroad, turning around anxieties over their solvency after the 1980s.
"Now reserves are almost big enough to cover Bradys -- these countries are not only solvent but also liquid," he said.
Luke said investors should hold onto their Brady bonds since the buy-back trend meant their value was likely to hold.

"If Latin America itself has the wherewithal and the willingness to buy back its debt, investors should defer to Latin America's judgement on the attraction of the investment and hold on." --London Newsroom +44 171 542 2734
